briefs.headline: Interests of charitable trust may differ from that of co: JP Morgan chairman & CEO Jamie Dimon
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: JP Morgan is the world’s most valuable bank, and its chairman and CEO Jamie Dimon is the longest serving chief of a large global bank. In an interview with TOI, Dimon speaks of what it takes to run America’s largest bank and his definition of success.
You completed two decades at JPMorgan this year. What does it take to run a bank successfully for two decades? Is it a conservative approach?
I took over Bank One in 2000 which effectively took control of JP Morgan, so it has been closer to 26 years. I consider myself conservative, but banking always involves risk. Good risk-taking is analytical, not guesswork: assess competitors, costs, capital, liquidity and stress scenarios.
You need to know the details, study the data and be honest about results. Success is not just profit; it’s about customers, products, execution and how you compare with the best. Have curiosity, courage and grit, and tell the board more about what went wrong than what went right. That is how you improve.
.
Ultimately, value matters, but a good company is more than profit. 
Are you retaining, hiring and training good people and building a culture of openness, curiosity and ambition across technology, products and systems? Maximising profit means little if products, systems or compliance fail and regulators are unhappy. You have to judge the whole business.
We’re seeing a lot of leadership changes in India. What should the objectives be for a CEO? Should it be just shareholder returns and customer satisfaction, or should it go beyond that?
It is about the whole institution: products, services, systems, people, culture, ethics and compliance. In India, that means serving clients while meeting govt and regulatory expectations. If a new system strengthens the business for 20 years, build it even if it hurts near-term profits or the share price. We also measure market share, competition and customer satisfaction because all three matter.
You introduced initiatives to help redevelop Detroit. Do you think that large institutions like JPMorgan should go beyond their role in just banking and look at benefiting society? And what’s the best structure for doing good?
Absolutely. It is part of our job. In India, we look to help lift the country through how we operate, serve our clients and raise capital. Since 2019, we’ve raised and provided clients with more than $84 billion in capital and credit. And since 2015, we have contributed more than $90 million in donations and helped more than 100,000 young people develop skills and access careers through our partnerships with nonprofits.
A healthy company helps clients and lifts society, and philanthropy must also deliver results. In Detroit, we made a multiyear commitment covering jobs, skills and healthcare, bringing all our businesses together. We learned from it and now apply the model in other cities. For CEOs, lifting society means doing both the commercial and philanthropic work.
In Detroit, we had a great leader in the mayor who said, “I’ll work with anybody who helps me.” He didn’t say, “I’m not going to speak to business. I’m not going to speak to philanthropy. I’m not going to speak to civil society.” He got everyone to the table to address basic needs such as housing, street lights, ambulances, policing, taxes and schools. He asked for help, acted on it and changed the city.
A lot of business houses in Europe and in India, like the Tatas, have a structure where they are owned by charitable trusts, and that’s the route used to do good. Do you think that is the right structure for doing good?
I’m not saying it’s always bad. A company should be run properly, and the interests of a charitable trust could be very different from the interests of a company. A company has got to be healthy and vibrant and have proper governance. A structure like that sometimes works against that.
I have seen boards in big American companies that are more obsessed with how they look than whether the company is building great products. And that is bad not just for the company, but for society. If the company isn’t healthy and vibrant, if it has the wrong goals, then it’s bad for jobs, capital formation and the country. So you’ve got to be quite careful with something like that.
I understand what you are referring to, and, to be clear, I think the world of Chandra. He’s done an extraordinary job in creating value for the foundations. Corporate governance is critical for a successful economy and its companies, and if changes are needed to corporate structures, they should be made.
When I walk into the boardroom, I ask the questions: “What’s the right thing to do for the company, its clients and the community?”
When do you think the Fed rate hike will start hurting and put stress on businesses?
At this point, it doesn’t, but at some point it will start to put stress. I don’t think the short rate is that important; I think it’s more about the 10-year rate. I don’t think one more 25-basis-point rate hike would do it. I’m very sympathetic to those facing stress, but I don’t put that in the systemic category.

briefs.headline: New Zealand trade pact to take effect on Oct 20, to give duty-free access
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: The India-New Zealand free trade agreement (FTA) will come into force on Oct 20 (Dusshera), providing duty-free access to 100% of India’s exports, commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal announced Monday. And, talks with Canada for a comprehensive economic partnership agreement (CEPA) are moving in top gear.
“The next 90 days should be a very defining period in the Canada-India relationship. Both sides have resolved to fast-track negotiations, in view of which our team is now slated to go for the fifth round on Oct 5,” Goyal told reporters. The fourth round of negotiations concluded on Sept 18 and the next one is scheduled in just around a fortnight, indicating that two sides are keen to clinch a deal soon. Canada is in the midst of a trade battle with the US and is seen to be keen to expand its trade footprint and reduce its reliance on its neighbour.
India’s major exports to Canada include pharmaceuticals, iron and steel, seafood, cotton garments, electronic goods and chemicals. Key imports from Canada include pulses, pearls and semi-precious stones, coal, fertilisers, paper and crude petroleum. Trade between the two countries stood at $30.4 billion in 2025, with an aim to double it to $70 billion by 2030. 
Besides, Goyal also expressed confidence regarding the trade pact with Chile. “In the coming few months, we will hear some good news,” he said.
Regarding the trade agreement with New Zealand, Goyal said it will help boost bilateral trade between the two countries to Rs 35,000 crore and will help facilitate $20 billion investments in India over next 15 years in sectors such as startups, manufacturing and infrastructure.
“We are taking forward the next important milestone in our bilateral economic partnership, reflecting our shared commitment to build a stronger and a more ambitious economic partnership,” Goyal said. The two countries had inked the pact in April this year.
Currently, New Zealand maintains tariffs of up to 10% on key Indian goods, including ceramics, carpets, automobiles, textiles and auto components. Goyal added that the pact also establishes an agricultural productivity partnership whereby New Zealand’s technology will meet India’s scale and growing demand.
For New Zealand, the pact will provide preferential access to the largest and fastest growing economy of the world, he said.

briefs.headline: Paramount reaches deal with states to settle their case challenging Warner buyout, AP source say
briefs.deck: ‘Today, billionaires have yet again bribed, censored, and bullied their way to the top,’ Alvaro Bedoya, senior adviser at the American Economic Liberties Project and former FTC commissioner, said in a statement
briefs.bodyText:
Skydance-owned Paramount reached a settlement on Monday (September 21, 2026) with a group of state attorneys general that had sued to challenge the company's buyout of Warner Bros. Discovery, effectively paving the way for the mega merger to move forward, a person familiar with the matter told the AP.
The person was not authorised to speak publicly and did so on condition of anonymity. Details of the settlement with the states were not immediately available, but were expected to be revealed later in the day.
The coalition of states — including entertainment heavyweights like California and New York — sued to block the $81 billion merger back in July, alleging a Paramount-Warner combo would “extinguish competition” and lead to fewer choices for consumers, particularly movie theatergoers and cable customers across the U.S.
Accompanied by a complaint also filed by the Writers Guild of America, the challenge was headed toward a full antitrust trial set to kick off in March.
Paramount said the allegations were meritless, but previously agreed to delay its transaction well into next year so the case could make its way through court. It then quickly called for a settlement — arguing that it had satisfied all regulatory clearances worldwide (including from the Trump administration's Justice Department) and the states' challenge was its “final obstacle.”
As reports of the states reaching a settlement with Paramount emerged Monday (September 21, 2026), critics decried the deal — while warning of what further consolidation could mean in an industry already controlled by just a few major players.
“Today, billionaires have yet again bribed, censored, and bullied their way to the top,” Alvaro Bedoya, senior adviser at the American Economic Liberties Project and former FTC commissioner, said in a statement earlier Monday (September 21, 2026).
“Layoffs will follow. People from L.A. to Atlanta will lose their jobs, small businesses will lose their contracts, your cable bill and movie ticket will be even more expensive.”

stories.headline: India vs Japan Live: Rain threat looms as India face Japan in historic one-off T20I
stories.bodyText:
Japan have waited for a moment like this, but the weather has already become a major concern. Heavy rain in Sano forced India to cancel their training session ahead of the one-off T20I.
The warning signs were already there. Japan’s match against Hong Kong on September 20, just two days before the India fixture, was abandoned without a ball being bowled.
The Japanese authorities will now hope the rain relents and the Sano facilities can withstand the conditions. A match against India is a huge occasion for Japanese cricket, and a washout would deny the home side a rare chance to take on the world champions.
VVS Laxman is back as India’s head coach for the Japan trip, and that makes the team selection interesting. Under Gautam Gambhir, India often went with three allrounders, giving them a batting option at No. 8 while slightly altering the balance of the bowling attack.
Laxman took a different approach in Zimbabwe, using four specialist bowlers. The Japan fixture could therefore offer an indication of how he wants to structure the side.
The probable XI includes Abhishek Sharma, Sanju Samson, Ishan Kishan, Shreyas Iyer, Tilak Varma, Axar Patel, Shivam Dube, Yash Thakur, Ravi Bishnoi, Arshdeep Singh and Jasprit Bumrah.
Facing Jasprit Bumrah is a daunting proposition for any batter. For Japan, it will also be a unique opportunity.
India have been carefully managing Bumrah’s workload, but the fast bowler has shown that he wants more game time, including his appearance in the dead rubber against Afghanistan. Now he could take the ball against Japan.
For Japan captain Kendel Kadowaki-Fleming and the rest of the batting line-up, facing Bumrah could provide an experience few international cricketers get. His variations, accuracy and pace will test Japan at a level they rarely encounter. It is a difficult challenge, but also a memorable one.
Tap to make your prediction
Kendel Kadowaki-Fleming will be one of the players attracting the most attention when Japan face India. The 30-year-old, born to a Japanese mother and Australian father, is Japan’s highest run-scorer in international cricket.
He also owns a remarkable T20 record. Alongside Lachlan Yamamoto-Lake, Kadowaki-Fleming put together an unbeaten 258-run partnership against China in 2024, the biggest partnership for any wicket in a T20 match.
He dropped himself to No. 3 in Japan’s recent match against Hong Kong, leaving open the question of where he will bat against India. Wherever he comes in, the captain will have a major role to play in Japan’s biggest cricketing occasion.
For Japan, this is not just another T20I. The country’s players are about to share a cricket field with the reigning world champions and some of the biggest names in the game.
Japan have made progress this year, beating Papua New Guinea in the Super Six stage of the T20 World Cup East Asia-Pacific Qualifiers. Now they face an entirely different challenge.
Jasprit Bumrah, Abhishek Sharma, Sanju Samson and other India stars will provide Japan with an invaluable learning experience. Technique, preparation, tactics and routines will all be on display. If Japan can make India work for their victory, this match could become one of the defining moments in their cricketing journey.
There is an unexpected link between India’s Japan trip and Don Bradman. When Australia travelled to England for the 1930 Ashes, the team stopped in Ceylon and played a day of cricket, with Bradman among the tourists. Ceylon was still decades away from becoming a Test nation.
Now India are making a similarly unusual cricketing detour. The world champions have travelled to Sano for a one-off T20I against Japan. The circumstances are obviously different, but the idea is remarkably similar: a leading cricket nation stopping off to play in a developing cricket country. For Japan, it is an occasion to remember.

stories.headline: 'Dhoni obviously plays a key role': CSK reveal thinking behind Zaheer Khan appointment
stories.deck: Zaheer Khan has stepped in as the new head coach for the Chennai Super Kings, a move significantly influenced by Mahendra Singh Dhoni. As a former left-arm pacer, Zaheer brings a wealth of experience to the franchise that has recently struggled. Honored by this opportunity, he eagerly anticipates playing a role in preserving and enhancing the team's illustrious legacy.
stories.bodyText:
Chennai: Mahendra Singh 
Dhoni
’s pinnacle as India captain was the 2011 World Cup triumph, and 
Zaheer Khan
 was one of that campaign’s unsung heroes. His joint-highest tally of 21 wickets in the tournament, alongside Pakistan skipper Shahid Afridi, and his opening spell of 5-3-6-1 in the final against Sri Lanka at the Wankhede are not celebrated as much as some of the other performances from that campaign.
Now, as Dhoni enters the final chapter of his playing career, he has turned to his trusted lieutenant as coach of 
Chennai Super Kings
, a team that has struggled to hit its customary heights over the last three seasons, failing to make the playoffs each time.
After Stephen Fleming’s exit as CSK coach, there was considerable speculation over his successor. The management left the decision largely to Dhoni. Several names were discussed, including Hemang Badani, but one understands that the former captain’s comfort level with Zaheer was among the key factors behind the former left-arm pacer landing the job.
Dhoni, as captain, had famously referred to Zaheer as the Sachin Tendulkar of bowling during India’s difficult 2012 World T20 campaign in Sri Lanka.
“Dhoni obviously plays a key role in our decision-making process. He, along with captain Ruturaj Gaikwad and other members of the cricket committee, concluded that Zaheer is the best man for the job,” CSK managing director Kasi Viswanathan told TOI.
CSK have struggled with their pace bowling lately, particularly at the death, and Zaheer’s mastery of reverse swing also worked in his favour.
“Zaheer was a world-class bowler and has mentored many young cricketers, especially fast bowlers, over the years. As a player, he was one of the key reasons for India’s success during the 2000s,” Viswanathan added.
Zaheer, on his part, said it was “an honour to be part of one of the most successful teams in the history of the IPL”.
“As a cricketer, I have faced CSK on the field and thoroughly enjoyed those contests. I can’t wait to join this legacy franchise with such a rich history,” he said.
The 47-year-old, who represented three IPL franchises (RCB, MI and DD) during his playing career, is no stranger to coaching.

briefs.headline: From Odisha’s villages to the Asian Games: The stories behind India’s women’s rugby squad
briefs.deck: In an exciting development, four talented players from Odisha will don the national colors for India in the upcoming Asian Games rugby sevens tournament. The experienced Dumuni Marndi will serve as vice-captain, leading a squad that also sees contributions from emerging rugby regions like Bihar. As the team prepares through rigorous training camps, they focus on both immediate success and…
briefs.bodyText:
Kolkata: Odisha’s rugby pipeline continues to power the Indian women’s sevens programme, with four players from the state earning selection in the squad for the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan.
Senior campaigner Dumuni Marndi (Mayurbhanj) will feature in her second Asian Games alongside Mama Naik (Keonjhar), Nirmalya Rout (Bargarh) and Sandhyarani Tudu (Baripada, Mayurbhanj).
For Marndi, the selection marks another chapter in a journey that began in rural Mayurbhanj, where her sporting ambitions were initially met with resistance at home.
“The last Asian Games was a huge learning experience. At that time, there were so many seniors around me that I could just focus on playing. Now there is more responsibility because I’m one of the senior players,” said the vice-captain.
The quartet’s inclusion is the latest testament to Odisha’s enduring influence on Indian rugby, with Sandhyarani Tudu among a long line of players to emerge from the state’s thriving grassroots system. She took up the sport after coaches introduced rugby at her school and believes Odisha’s strong culture has been central to its success.
“Rugby is doing very well in Odisha. We consistently win medals and our team bonding is very strong. That has helped many players come through,” said Sandhyarani, a fly-half known for her tackling, passing and game awareness.
Former age-group captain Mama Naik has also emerged as one of India’s brightest forward prospects, while Nirmalya Rout adds leadership credentials after captaining Odisha to the 2026 senior nationals crown.
But even as Odisha continues to produce national team regulars, the sport is spreading across newer regions as well. Bihar, for instance, has two players in the squad.
One of them is Arti Kumari, who continues to draw inspiration from her elder brother Rahul Kumar, who died in an accident in 2020.
“My brother was my biggest supporter. He always encouraged me to chase my dreams,” said Arti, who hails from Nawada.
Fellow Bihar player Guriya Kumari, from Muzaffarpur, has overcome a very different challenge. The youngster battled back from an ACL injury that required two surgeries on the same leg.
“There was a time when I thought I would never be able to play again,” Guriya recalled.
However, she has put all that behind her and is focused on the Asiad, where India will play its Pool B opener against Hong Kong on Oct. 1 at Paloma Mizuho Rugby Stadium. India's remaining two pool games will be against defending champions China and Malaysia.
While head coach Paul Delport expects a stern test at the Asian Games, he is taking confidence from India’s recent performance at Asia Rugby Emirates Sevens Series, where the team finished sixth after recording victories over UAE and Iran. India also had a preparatory camp in Thailand, where they played practice matches against the hosts and Sri Lanka.
“The players have improved enormously, both physically and in terms of game understanding. Considering how few tournaments we’re able to play, the progress has been exceptional,” Delport said of the team that finished seventh in the last Asiad.
The former South Africa international, however, insisted that the focus must remain on the process rather than the results. Rugby India president Rahul Bose also echoed that sentiment, arguing that progress in team sports often takes longer to become visible on the scoreboard.
But with an eye on the 2032 Olympics, Bose reiterated the need to create a more professional ecosystem for players.
“We have to make rugby fully professional. You cannot just have camps and send players home. Centres of excellence and year-round programmes are the way forward,” he said in Kolkata on Monday.
While Bose hinted that some of those plans could begin taking shape in the coming months, the immediate focus remains the Asian Games for which the team departs on Friday.

briefs.headline: Asian Games chaos! Typhoon Dujuan disrupts equestrian; India’s schedule cut short
briefs.deck: The Asian Games equestrian eventing competition faced a delay due to Typhoon Dujuan, necessitating the rescheduling of the dressage and cross-country events to Tuesday. In light of safety protocols, Indian riders have been instructed to stay indoors. Concerns about communication from the chef-de-equipe were raised, as India strives to uphold its dressage gold medal amid this tumultuous situation.
briefs.bodyText:
New Delhi: Typhoon Dujuan cast a shadow over the Asian Games on Monday, forcing organisers to postpone the opening day of the equestrian eventing competition at Tokyo Equestrian Park as a precaution against worsening weather.
The dressage phase, involving India’s riders, was called off after organisers grew wary of heavy rain and strong winds that could make conditions unsafe. An Indian rider told TOI that the decision was taken as a safety measure and riders were asked to stay indoors before returning to their designated team hotel.
The postponement has squeezed the three-day programme into two days. Dressage and cross-country will now be held on Tuesday, with jumping scheduled for Wednesday.
While swimming and cycling continued largely unaffected in Tokyo city, the outdoor equestrian competition bore the brunt of the approaching storm.
The Japan Meteorological Agency warned that Dujuan could bring intense rain, strong winds and flooding to eastern Japan. Heavy rain is expected to persist into Tuesday.
Meanwhile, some Indian riders have raised concerns over communications from chef-de-equipe, Lt Col Sandeep Dewan. 
Riders alleged that while Dewan was attending official delegation meetings, information from those meetings was not being shared with them.
They also said they were not consulted about attending the opening ceremony. Riders stressed that the order of go should first be discussed among athletes and the coach before being finalised and conveyed to the chef-de-equipe.
The concerns come with India seeking to defend its dressage gold from the previous Asian Games, as the competition resumes amid challenging weather.

briefs.headline: Irish athletes’ group urges national team to boycott Israel fixtures
briefs.deck: Ireland are due to ⁠play Israel on September 27 in Hungary before the reverse fixture in Serbia on October 4
briefs.bodyText:
More than 160 Irish sportspeople have signed an open letter asking the Ireland national football team to boycott their upcoming UEFA Nations League fixtures against Israel, the Irish Sport for Palestine Group said on Monday (September 2026).
Ireland are due to play Israel on September 27 in Hungary before the reverse fixture in Serbia on October 4. Both matches are set to be staged at neutral venues and behind closed doors after protests by players and fans over the death toll of Palestinian civilians during the war in Gaza.
Irish Sport for Palestine said the signatories included Olympian Ciara Mageean, former footballer Louise Quinn, former rugby flyhalf Tony Ward and boxers Tyrone McKenna and Eric Donovan.
"This is a significant moment and with this moment you have an opportunity to do the right thing," the letter said.
"Not playing the game would be the most sporting thing you could do. Through your leadership and courage, it would show the power of sport to unite, remind us of the shared values that connect us all, and have an impact far beyond the game."
In May, leading Irish footballers joined celebrities in a campaign urging Ireland to boycott the Nations League matches against Israel.
Ireland has been one of the European Union's most outspoken critics of Israel's war in Gaza, and Football Association of Ireland (FAI) members voted overwhelmingly in late 2025 for its board to request that UEFA immediately suspend the Israel Football Association from European competitions.
The FAI later committed to playing the fixtures, citing possible sanctions that could affect the national team and the association.
Ireland coach Heimir Hallgrimsson said last week he had spoken individually to players about facing Israel and that "none of us feel comfortable playing in these games".
Reuters has contacted the Israeli FA for comment.

briefs.headline: Infantino proposes consulting federations to reform FIFA
briefs.deck: ‘I will propose that the Council establish a direct, structured and time-limited consultation with confederations, Member Associations and relevant stakeholders on how FIFA’s decision-making can be further strengthened,’ Infantino wrote
briefs.bodyText:
FIFA president Gianni Infantino on Monday (September 21, 2026) suggested a "consultation" with the member federations to reform the world football governing body's decision-making processes, in a letter addressed to the 211 member associations, as seen by AFP.
"I will propose that the Council establish a direct, structured and time-limited consultation with confederations, Member Associations and relevant stakeholders on how FIFA's decision-making can be further strengthened," Infantino wrote.
The 56-year-old Swiss has come under fire since his now-abandoned plan to bring private investment into the men's and women's World Cups.
"The consultation would invite specific proposals on earlier institutional involvement, the respective roles of the President, the Bureau, the Council and the Congress, and practical ways to strengthen transparency, participation and accountability in major strategic initiatives," the letter continued.
Infantino asked for the initial proposals to be considered at the council meeting scheduled for October 15, 2026.
Infantino replaced Sepp Blatter as president of FIFA in 2016. He has come under severe pressure since the announcement in late July of proposals to create a commercial subsidiary to run its biggest events, such as the World Cup and Club World Cup.
The plan would have allowed private investors to acquire stakes in a company created under the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) initiative. The backlash that followed led to the proposals being quickly shelved.
European football's governing body UEFA threatened to boycott FIFA competitions. It later suspended that threat, but has urged Infantino to resign and has been preparing possible legal action against him for alleged "criminal mismanagement".
Infantino addressed FFE in his letter on Monday (September 21) and wrote that "FIFA's democratic processes, independence and sporting authority were never for sale".
The plan also "did not involve relinquishing FIFA's control or authority over sporting decisions", he insisted.
‘Clear and trusted’
He further lamented the fact that the scheme "entered the public domain before FIFA's planned institutional process had been completed and before it could be presented in full to the Council and the Member Associations".
"I recognise that, without the full context, this caused concern and created the impression that decisions had already been taken. They had not," Infantino added.
"Major ideas must be developed, tested and communicated through clear and trusted institutions. That is a responsibility I take seriously."
UEFA, alongside the North American body CONCACAF and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), issued a no-holds-barred joint letter against Infantino in August.
"Leadership in football is not a possession. It is not about holding — or demanding — power to be held," they wrote.
However, Infantino is not without friends — 2034 World Cup hosts Saudi Arabia came out in support last month, with African football's governing body CAF and South America's CONMEBOL also supportive.
FIFA confirmed earlier in September that Infantino will stand for re-election as president next March.
At this stage, he is the only candidate. However, CONCACAF president Victor Montagliani is widely seen as a likely challenger.
Candidate nominations for next year's election must be submitted by November 18.

briefs.headline: Rudrankksh —Indian shooting’s ‘chosen one’
briefs.deck: The 22-year-old, who clinched bronze in 10m air rifle at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, has overcome a dark phase with constant learning and determination; the versatile shooter hopes to ‘complete the set’ at the 2028 Olympics
briefs.bodyText:
Three years ago, Rudrankksh Balasaheb Patil was being spoken of, in hushed but awed tone, as a possible successor to Abhinav Bindra.
The then 19-year-old’s performances and consistency had evoked admiration and hope in the shooting fraternity. But it all came crashing when he stumbled, finishing fourth in 10m air rifle at the 2023 Asian Games and failing to make the cut for the Paris Olympics — a quota he had held on to for two years after becoming the first Indian shooter to earn one. It wasn’t his skill that let him down; it was the mind. Still only 22, Rudrankksh is now a lot more in control — of his mind, emotions, thoughts. That control saw him go one better on his disappointing Hangzhou outing, winning a bronze medal in 10m air rifle in Aichi-Nagoya.
Most importantly, the teenaged nervous energy has been replaced by a quietly confident one, a belief that he is good enough to succeed in not one but two events. He is representing India in both 10m air rifle and 50m rifle 3-Positions, the latter an addition after the Paris heartbreak in 2024.
Getting inspired
“As I see it, there are only a couple of athletes in the world who are doing well in two events. There are a lot of myths around balancing the two. When I started, there was a belief that if you do a second event, it will destroy your 10m form. There is also a thought that it’s difficult to manage both.
“But I was told by my nutritionist and psychologist that as long as you have two working legs and two working hands, you can do multiple events. That inspired me. And I saw Michael Phelps, who participated in multiple events and won multiple medals in all of them. So why not me? I have age on my side. I have a lot of years to make mistakes and learn through them,” the bespectacled youngster said in an exclusive interaction with The Hindu during the preparatory camp in Bhopal.
“This is the first Asian Games where I am participating in two events. It’s my fourth international competition doing so. Every time, I have improved a little bit. I have good coaches, good support staff. There is a lot of motivation. The hunger and greed is intact: if anything, it’s grown,” he added.
Content with third place
He has definitely learned. The bronze, which he clinched in 10m air rifle after leading for almost 70% of the competition here on Monday, might have been a disappointment at another time but for someone who has been in this position before, a medal was more than welcome.
“I am very happy with bronze because a lot of things could have gone wrong but all of it ended well. I would like to see the positives rather than the negatives,” he said.
The aftermath of missing out on an Olympic outing was big, but for those around him more than himself. He hadn’t done badly: he finished third behind Arjun Babuta and Sandeep Singh in the trials.
“The sad part was seeing my parents and support staff. I was fine, honestly. My initial thought was: ‘I competed in 13 events and won 11. It’s just this one match that I lost, not a big deal’. But when I realised everyone was looking forward to that one match and were sad after watching me work hard, I was affected.
“I was actually sad because all the hard work which I had put in did not yield the result. But then, I started seeing the facts. It’s not that I was not selected because my score was bad: it was because one person shot a really high score. And I could not compete with that. Secondly, I always evaluate what I could have done better after a competition... the mistakes I made. But after that, I had nothing. I had given my best, my everything. I was able to figure things out and move forward.
“I started in a new event. My way of taking a break was getting back to shooting but it was on my terms. I used to go to the range but with no set schedule. I trained as I liked, whenever or however I liked... sometimes for hours, sometimes maybe for just 15 to 20 minutes. It was just a part of my life in which I had to be patient, I had to be persistent. I gradually built up my love for the sport again and started enjoying it,” Rudrankksh explained the dark phase.
Finishing the job
There is also a determination to see his dreams, hard work and journey through to the end. It’s something that drives him, considering the fear of leaving things midway has happened far too often for comfort.
“When I started my sporting journey, I was not exactly in a happy space in life. My marks (academics) were just fine, I was not good in other sports, I was new to the city and did not have many friends, I was lagging in everything. My parents used to get me some mechanical or Lego sets and I never completed any.
“It was a recurring complaint from my teachers, that I was not completing anything. It became an obsession for me, it became a fixation that I want to do something in my life. I want to complete something. I started seeing athletes all over... Phelps. I had watched Bindra sir’s 2016 Olympics in Rio. All those sparked something in me. Even now, whenever things are not working out, I look around me for inspiration.
“A lot of athletes show up every day. Manu Bhaker, who is always on time, everywhere, always in the gym no matter what. Maybe, someone some day is as inspired by me as I am by others. That thought keeps me alive, gives me hope.”
He has learnt to stop worrying about things not in his control. Call it fate or luck, but Rudrankksh prefers calling himself the ‘chosen one’ for all the unexpected setbacks he has faced, many of them not of his making. “I am kind of used to it by now. Even today (Monday), after my match was done, I picked up my rifle and the strap of the case broke. At the Peru World Cup, my gun auto-fired in the final and I was eliminated. Only my visa gets rejected,” he shrugged.
Showing maturity
The nervous, high-strung energy has settled into a quieter rhythm. It had helped him perform back then but had taken a toll on his health, both physical and mental. He suffered an auto-immune condition triggered by stress, messed up his sleep cycle and was desperate to continue regardless of everything — a lot like being on a high without drugs.
“When I lost, I would be down in the dumps. When I won, I used to feel like wanting to continue the streak no matter what — whether my sleep was affected, my hands were shaking, I was tired and ready to drop dead. Nothing mattered, only winning did. It has changed now but I am still learning how my body works. I learnt that fatigue is something which builds up during the Olympic time. I know I need to be more strategic and dissociated from the results.”
He knows he will make mistakes. He also knows that he will keep learning from them. Like Monday, when he admitted that slipping from No. 1 to No. 3 was largely his own doing — a poor 9.7 shot dashed his golden hopes.
“This gives me a kick, reminding me that I need to be calm till the last moment. I was too excited for the shot and I released before calming down. I think all the accumulated things over the last six months... perhaps it was just the way the body reacted once a medal was confirmed. The last time I spoke to you, I said I was looking to improve my rank, and that’s exactly what happened. Perhaps I need to watch what comes out of my mouth the next time,” he quipped.
External support
The support from the system has played a big role in his growth in 50m 3P. “The TOPS CEO then (Cmdr. P.K. Garg) was very supportive. He sanctioned my trip to Serbia for training with Olympic medallist Milenko Sebic. And he was impressed. The National coaches guided me on the right equipment, ammunition suppliers and provided the shots. Everything came together and in 2025, I participated in my first trials. I was in top-10, then top-6, now top-3. I hope to continue this.”
He is also aware that there is a long way to go. Aishwary Pratap Singh Tomar, who beat him in the shoot-off for the 10m bronze medal in Hangzhou, is the top guy in 50m 3P. While Rudrankksh insists that there is no rivalry between the two, he is clear on the strengths of both.
“I don’t and can’t compare myself with him in 3P because he is the best in the country for the past seven to eight years. This year, I was able to play with him in three international tournaments: my aim every time was to score around 587 points while he shot above 590 in all. I don’t compare myself with him in 10m because I feel I am better. I have proved myself in it more than him and I have been in the 10m team for as long as he’s been in 3P. But yes, there are times when he shoots 10m better than everyone. In fact, he is also one of my inspirations to try two events — if he can do it, why can’t I?”
The Asian Games will help him complete the first set of targets he has set for himself, a list that, by his own admission, has grown in reverse. From being crowned the World champion in 10m air rifle in his maiden senior international outing in 2022 to winning his first National title earlier this year, Rudrankksh’s journey has been interesting, to say the least.
“I won the World championship, then the World Cup Final, World Cups, got the World No. 1 title, the World Record. This year, I won the Asian championship for the first time after finishing fourth repeatedly. The only regret is that despite all this, I have not even been considered for an Arjuna Award so far. I even won my first National-level tournament this year. But there is the Olympics to complete the set, maybe they will recognise after that,” he signed off.

briefs.headline: Yashbardhan slams another ton as India u-19 clinches series
briefs.bodyText:
There’s no stopping Yashbardhan Singh Chauhan. After his all-round effort earned him the Player-of-the-Match award in the series opener, he followed it up with a 100-ball 122 (15x4, 2x6) to help India u-19 beat Australia u-19 by 102 runs and take an unassailable 2-0 lead in the three-match Youth ODI series.
At the Niranjan Shah Stadium on Monday, India u-19 opted to bat on a flat deck and made the most of it. Aaryavir Sehwag set the tone early, beginning with a boundary.
Aaryavir scored 47 before a mix-up with V.K. Vineeth (87, 92b, 4x4, 6x6) ended his innings. The pair added 55 for the second wicket before Yashbardhan took over. Initially watchful, Yashbardhan gradually opened up, playing predominantly in the ‘V’ and eventually finding the gaps with ease. His innings provided the backbone to India’s 341 for seven.
Australia’s chase began poorly, with Mohit Ulva and C. Venkata reducing it to 29 for two. Jack Czosnek (81, 63b, 7x4, 4x6) and Blake Cattle (44) added 99 for the fourth wicket to revive the chase.
Once the partnership was broken, Australia’s resistance faded.

briefs.headline: CSK names Zaheer Khan as head coach for IPL 2027
briefs.deck: The former Indian pacer replaces Kiwi Stephen Fleming who guided the Men in Yellow from 2009 to 2026
briefs.bodyText:
CChennai Super Kings (CSK) has appointed former India pacer Zaheer Khan as its head coach for IPL 2027. Zaheer replaces Stephen Fleming who guided the Men in Yellow from 2009 to 2026.
The former New Zealand skipper was removed from the job earlier this year after three poor seasons for the five-time champion, in which it failed to qualify for the playoffs.
One-year deal
Interestingly, Zaheer will be on a one-year contract.
With the mega auction set to take place before 2028, it remains to be seen if this is a short-term arrangement.
Zaheer has previously been part of the coaching set-up with Mumbai Indians and Lucknow Super Giants.
Rupa Gurunath, owner, CSK, said: “We are pleased to confirm Zaheer as the head coach. Zaheer’s distinguished playing career and proven ability to nurture young talent make him a valuable addition to our set-up. We are confident that his guidance will help strengthen the core of the franchise.”
K.S. Viswanathan, Managing Director, CSK, said Zaheer will have the freedom to choose his own support staff.
“Zaheer is a world-class bowler and has been a mentor to many young cricketers, especially fast bowlers, over the years. He’s one of the finest cricketing brains, and we look forward to having him in our family.”
Zaheer said: “It’s an honour to be a part of one of the most successful teams in the IPL. I have faced CSK on the field and have thoroughly enjoyed the contests. The atmosphere created by the superfans at Chepauk makes it even more special. I can’t wait to join the franchise with such a rich history”.
